title: Reading the Apocalypse
hook: apocalypse means unveiling: a letter of hope to churches under pressure

segments.voice: Yesterday, the letters ended with Jude's doxology. Your line was able to keep you.

Say apocalypse and most people picture the end of the world: burning cities, empty highways, a zombie movie. Now go back to the date tradition gives, near the end of the first century. You're in a small group of Christians meeting in a house, in a city in what is now western Turkey. The empire expects everyone to honor the emperor, and some of your people have paid for refusing. One Sunday a letter arrives from a man named John, on an island called Patmos. It's full of trumpets, beasts, a dragon and a city of gold. And it's addressed to you.
screen: `APOCALYPSE: THE MOVIE VERSION.` → `A HOUSE CHURCH IN ASIA.` → `A LETTER FROM PATMOS.`

segments.voice: Apocalypse is the book's first word in Greek, apokalypsis: an uncovering, the veil pulled off. That's why some Bibles call the book Revelation, and the Douay-Rheims calls it the Apocalypse. Same word. Its first line calls it the revelation of Jesus Christ, shown to his servant John. So what's unveiled? Not mainly a timetable. Mostly, what's really going on behind what you can see. On the surface, Rome looks invincible and the little churches look finished. Pull back the curtain, and there's a throne in heaven, a Lamb who was slain and stands alive, and worship that never stops. It's a letter of hope to churches under pressure. It's also a particular kind of writing, like parts of the book of Daniel: dreams, visions, numbers and creatures that stand for something. Readers have long taken seven as a sign of completeness. And the book opens with a promise: "Blessed is he, that readeth and heareth the words of this prophecy." A book meant to be read aloud, in church. Christians read it in different ways: as history told in advance, as mostly about the first century, or as symbols for every age. Catholic teaching reads it on more than one level at once: a word to those first churches, a word to the Church in every time, and a hope for the end, when Christ comes again. The Church doesn't hand out a calendar of the last days. It hands out the book itself, read at Mass in the Easter season and as the Church year closes.
screen: `APOKALYPSIS: PULLING OFF THE VEIL.` · `WHAT'S REALLY GOING ON.` · `VISIONS, NUMBERS, CREATURES.` · `READ ALOUD, ON MORE THAN ONE LEVEL.` · then, large: `AN UNVEILING, NOT AN ENDING.`

segments.voice: Open the last book, in a Bible or an app, and read chapter one slowly, aloud if you can, the way it was first heard. Don't decode anything; notice what stays with you, a voice like many waters, a right hand laid on someone afraid. Without the text, picture that house church hearing it for the first time; if you pray, ask to see what's behind the veil.
Apocalypse. From the Greek for unveiling: pulling the cover off what's really going on. The last book of the Bible. Today's word.
Your line: an unveiling. Thirteen days in the last book start here. Day six hundred nineteen, done.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the Apocalypse at Mass, especially in the Easter season and in the last weeks of the Church year, and its hymns run through the Liturgy of the Hours; the Church reads it as a book of hope in Christ's victory rather than a timetable for the end.
